Can't give you a definite answer but I suspect it's mostly just separation of the ingredients.

To make mayo, take a cup of olive oil (extra light tasting, if you're actually going to use this to make mayo), a large egg and a tablespoon of lemon juice and mix them together with a hand blender (magic bullet, immersion blender, whatever) by placing the blender at the bottom of the container, turning it on and slowly pulling upwards. Add salt/spices to taste.

This turns 3 ingredients, of which only the egg yolk is opaque and transforms it into the opaque-white mayonnaise. Leaving it sitting out in warm temperatures might be causing them to separate into the original ingredients which makes the mayo mostly clear again.

Mayonnaise is an emulsion -- a fine dispersion of minute droplets of one liquid in another in which it is not soluble or miscible. In mayo's case it's between oil and vinegar/lemon juice. To keep it emulsified you need an emulsifier. For mayo this comes in the form of lecithin which is found in the egg yolk (which is also part of the recipe).

I believe mayo goes transparent when left out because the emulsion is breaking down and the components are starting to separate. I can think of two mechanisms for this. Either water is evaporating out just leaving the oil behind or perhaps the lecithin or some other component is oxidizing causing the emulsion to separate. Tempature does't seem to play a huge role in it (sealed jars of mayo keep at room temperature for months). It's exposure to air causes it (so either evaporation or oxidation). At least that's my theory.
